:::{#thm-rank-product-right}
#### Multiplying on the left cannot increase the rank

If $\matr{A}$ is $m \times n$ and $\matr{B}$ is $n \times k$, then

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A} \matr{B}) \le \operatorname{rank}(\matr{B}).
$$

:::

::: proof

$$
\ba
\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A} \matr{B})
&= \operatorname{rank}(\tp{(\matr{A} \matr{B})})
&& \text{(@thm-rank-transpose)}
\\
&= \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{B}}\,\tp{\matr{A}})
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&\le \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{B}})
&& \text{(@thm-rank-product, with } \tp{\matr{B}} \text{ on the left)}
\\
&= \operatorname{rank}(\matr{B}).
&& \text{(@thm-rank-transpose)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-product-right}
#### A product of rank 1 with a factor of rank 2

Let

$$
\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\matr{A} \matr{B}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 & 1 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 0 \\ 0 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 & 0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 0 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

$\matr{A}$ has rank $2$, because its columns $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ are linearly independent.
$\matr{B}$ has rank $1$, because its second column is $\vzero_2$ and its first is not,
and $\matr{A} \matr{B}$ has rank $1$ for the same reason.
So $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A} \matr{B}) = 1 \le \operatorname{rank}(\matr{B}) = 1$ (@thm-rank-product-right),
and the bound of @thm-rank-product, $2$, is not the tighter one.

:::
